atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to assess the comparative efficacy and safety of canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin in adults with type 2 diabetes.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Aim: To assess the comparative efficacy and safety of sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors in adults with type 2 diabetes.

atoms.canonical_statement: The investigators conducted a systematic review and frequentist network meta-analysis according to a prespecified protocol and PRISMA/network-meta-analysis reporting guidance.
PubMed, ISI Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through 3 November 2015 without language restriction.
Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in adults with type 2 diabetes lasting at least 24 weeks and reporting at least one prespecified cardiometabolic or safety outcome.

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes represented in the included randomized controlled trials
inclusion_criteria: At least one prespecified cardiometabolic or safety outcome

atoms.canonical_statement: Trials that included only patients with chronic kidney disease at baseline were excluded.

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes represented in the included randomized controlled trials
exclusion_criteria: Only patients with chronic kidney disease at baseline

atoms.canonical_statement: Licensed canagliflozin doses evaluated were 100 mg and 300 mg.
Licensed dapagliflozin doses evaluated were 5 mg and 10 mg.
Licensed empagliflozin doses evaluated were 10 mg and 25 mg.
The network included placebo and active glucose-lowering comparators; linagliptin and sitagliptin were grouped as DPP-4 inhibitors.

exposures.details: Linagliptin and sitagliptin were combined in the review network.

atoms.canonical_statement: Glimepiride and gliclazide were grouped as sulphonylureas in the network.

exposures.details: Glimepiride and gliclazide were combined in the review network.

atoms.canonical_statement: Three authors independently performed the literature search and independently extracted data with standardized predefined forms; disagreements were resolved by arbitration.
When published reports did not provide extractable data, the investigators retrieved relevant information from ClinicalTrials.gov.
Study quality was assessed with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool.
Pairwise random-effects meta-analyses used the DerSimonian-Laird method.
Network meta-analysis used a frequentist multivariate meta-analysis framework with a common heterogeneity variance across treatment contrasts.
Dichotomous outcomes were summarized as odds ratios and a 0.5 continuity correction was added when a study reported zero events.
Network consistency was evaluated with the design-by-treatment interaction model.
For missing contrasts in three-arm continuous-outcome trials, the main analysis assumed a correlation of 0.5; sensitivity analyses using 0.2, 0.7, and 0.9 produced similar results.
The review included 38 unique randomized controlled trials with 23,997 participants.

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes represented in the included randomized controlled trials

atoms.canonical_statement: The included trials were published from 2012 through 2015, had follow-up durations from 24 to 208 weeks, and enrolled 136 to 2,072 participants per trial.

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes represented in the included randomized controlled trials

atoms.canonical_statement: Weighted baseline characteristics across included trials were HbA1c 8.1%, age 58 years, diabetes duration 8 years, and 57% male.

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes represented in the included randomized controlled trials

atoms.canonical_statement: Overall Cochrane risk-of-bias judgments were 89.5% low risk, 1.8% high risk, and 8.7% unclear risk across assessed domains.
High or unclear domain-specific risk of bias was reported in 1.8% of canagliflozin trials, 10.8% of dapagliflozin trials, and 16.7% of empagliflozin trials.

atoms.canonical_statement: The meta-analysis was study-level and relied on journal publications or ClinicalTrials.gov rather than individual-participant data.
Some outcomes were missing or not extractable in individual trials, producing outcome-specific evidence networks rather than one common denominator.
Participant ethnicity, follow-up duration, and outcome selection, definition, and ascertainment varied across trials.

The body-weight evidence network showed statistically significant inconsistency in the full analysis (p=0.0229), although this inconsistency was absent in the 24–30 week sensitivity network (p=0.386).
No direct head-to-head randomized trials compared the evaluated SGLT2 inhibitors, so comparative differences among agents were inferred through the treatment network.
The authors concluded that SGLT2 inhibitors improved cardiometabolic markers in type 2 diabetes but increased genital-infection risk.
The authors concluded that canagliflozin 300 mg generally performed better than the other evaluated SGLT2 inhibitor doses for cardiometabolic markers.
The authors called for randomized direct SGLT2 comparisons and cardiovascular-outcome trials to clarify whether biomarker differences translate into different long-term outcomes.

The authors acknowledged support from NIHR Collaboration for Leadership in Applied Health Research and Care – East Midlands, the Leicester Clinical Trials Unit, and the NIHR Leicester-Loughborough Diet, Lifestyle and Physical Activity Biomedical Research Unit.
